titleStmt.title: Does the Media Matter? A Field Experiment Measuring the Effect of Newspapers on Voting Behavior and Political Opinions
titleStmt.author: Alan S Gerber
Dean Karlan
Daniel E. Bergan

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Does the Media Matter? A Field Experiment Measuring the Effect of Newspapers on Voting Behavior and Political Opinions

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our investigation of the effect of newspapers on political attitudes, behavior, and subject knowledge of news events found that even short exposure to a daily newspaper appears to influence voting behavior and may affect turnout behavior.

span.label: media effects on voting behavior
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Online processing: readers update their candidate evaluations as information arrives but do not retain the facts that moved them, which is why opinions shift while measured knowledge does not
span.quote: political scientists have constructed models of online processing of political information, where citizens update their judgments in response to the flow of information but do not retain memory of the particular facts that caused them to revise their views

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Shared content beats slant: both papers covered war casualties and administration scandals during a period bad for Republicans, so what the two papers had in common moved readers in the same direction
span.quote: It may be that what the coverage had in common was more important than any differences between the newspapers.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Continued exposure after the election — leftover subscription weeks plus voluntary renewals — carries the treatment forward and explains why turnout moved in 2006 but not 2005
span.quote: This could be a result of the post-election receipt of the remainder of the ten-week newspaper subscriptions or the treatment that resulted from the 17 percent of the Post treatment group who renewed their subscription after the free period ended.

span.label: Small sample, so treatment effects are estimated imprecisely.
span.note: what this limits: the precision of every treatment effect: THE MOST IMPORTANT [limitation] OF WHICH IS THE RELATIVELY SMALL SAMPLE SIZE
span.quote: Our study has some important limitations, the most important of which is the relatively small sample size.

span.label: Delivery was randomised but actual reading could not be verified.
span.note: what this limits: the interpretation of the treatment itself: WE KNOW WHICH HOUSEHOLDS RECEIVED NEWSPAPERS, [but] WE CANNOT BE SURE THAT THE NEWSPAPERS WERE READ
span.quote: One limitation of this study is that while we know which households received newspapers, we cannot be sure that the newspapers were read.

span.label: Attrition on unobservables could bias the estimates.
span.note: what this limits: the unbiasedness of the estimates: IF THERE IS ATTRITION BASED ON UNOBSERVED VARIABLES THAT ARE CORRELATED WITH THE OUTCOME MEASURES BUT NOT PREDICTED BY THE OBSERVABLES, OUR RESULTS MAY BE BIASED
span.quote: If there is attrition based on unobserved variables that are correlated with the outcome measures but not predicted by the observables, our results may be biased.

span.label: The sample frame excludes existing subscribers, so the estimated effect applies to an unusually low-media-exposure population.
span.note: what this limits: the population the effect applies to: WE ARE STUDYING INDIVIDUALS WHO DO NOT ALREADY SUBSCRIBE TO A NEWSPAPER, HENCE ARE EXAMINING THE EFFECT OF EXPOSING INDIVIDUALS WHO, ON AVERAGE, ARE LESS EXPOSED TO THE MEDIA THAN THE A[verage]
span.quote: We are studying individuals who do not already subscribe to a newspaper, hence are examining the effect of exposing individuals who, on average, are less exposed to the media than the average individual.

span.label: The turnout effect appeared only in 2006 and was of borderline significance, so both the effect and its mechanism are held provisional.
span.note: what this limits: the turnout result specifically: BOTH THE EXISTENCE OF AN EFFECT AND ITS POTENTIAL MECHANISM SHOULD BE TREATED GUARDEDLY UNTIL FURTHER STUDY
span.quote: Therefore, both the existence of an effect and its potential mechanism should be treated guardedly until further study.

span.label: What was randomised is delivery, not reading: the authors state they cannot be sure the newspapers were read.
span.note: what this limits: reading the estimates as effects of newspaper EXPOSURE: the randomisation assigned delivery, and the authors state they cannot be sure the papers were read
span.quote: One limitation of this study is that while we know which households received newspapers, we cannot be sure that the newspapers were read.

span.label: The authors name small sample size as their most important limitation, with consequences for the standard errors.
span.note: what this limits: treating a null result here as evidence of no effect: the authors name the relatively small sample size as their most important limitation, with 1,081 survey interviews and 2,571 merged records
span.quote: Our study has some important limitations, the most important of which is the relatively small sample size. The sample size for the post-election survey was 1,081 interviews and the sample size for the data merged with administrative voting records is still only 2,571.

span.label: The orthogonality claim is conditional: unobservables correlated with the outcome but unpredicted by the observables would still bias the result.
span.note: what this limits: the randomisation as guaranteeing unbiasedness of these particular estimates: the authors state results may still be biased through unobservables not predicted by the observed covariates
span.quote: based on unobserved variables that are correlated with the outcome measures but not predicted by the observables, our results may be biased.

span.label: Just under a third of the assigned sample supplied the survey outcomes.
span.note: what this limits: the follow-up survey as covering the assigned sample: 1,081 of the 3,347 individuals were reinterviewed for it
span.quote: During the week after the November election, we reinterviewed 1,081 of the 3,347 individuals in our sample for the follow-up survey.

span.label: WHAT WAS RANDOMISED IS DELIVERY, NOT READING, and the authors say so plainly: they know which households received newspapers but cannot be sure the newspapers were read. The treatment the design controls is not the treatment the theory is about, and the gap is bridged by three self-reported survey measures.
span.quote: One limitation of this study is that while we know which households received newspapers, we cannot be sure that the newspapers were read

span.label: The online-processing model of attitude formation, taken from psychological work on impression formation and persuasion, is used to explain why candidate preference moved without any measurable gain in factual knowledge
span.quote: Drawing on work from psychology (Norman H. Anderson and Stephen Hubert 1963, and W. A. Watts and W. J. McGuire 1964), political scientists have constructed models of online processing of political information

span.label: households randomly assigned to a third arm that was sent NEITHER newspaper, alongside the Post and Times subscription arms
span.note: eliminates: prior political interest and everything else that differs between people who read a paper and people who do not - random assignment makes the untreated arm comparable in expectation, which observational media studies cannot do
span.quote: we randomly assigned households to get subscriptions to either the Post or the Times for approximately ten weeks, or to a control group that was not sent either paper

span.label: media slant
span.quote: We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure.

span.label: field experiment
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion.

span.label: newspaper provision
span.quote: Our follow-up survey provides three measures of the effect of newspaper provision on newspaper reading

span.label: media exposure
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion. Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment. We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure. Some evidence from voting records also suggests that receiving either paper led to increased 2006 voter turnout

span.label: turnout
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion. Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment. We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure. Some evidence from voting records also suggests that receiving either paper led to increased 2006 voter turnout

span.label: treatment - AS ASSIGNMENT: which households were sent a free subscription, which is the thing actually randomised
span.quote: we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment.

span.label: treatment - AS EXPOSURE: whether the newspaper was read, which the paper states it cannot be sure of and can only proxy through three survey measures
span.quote: Our follow-up survey provides three measures of the effect of newspaper provision on newspaper reading: whether subjects receive a newspaper, which newspaper they receive, and the frequency with which they read a newspaper

span.label: media effect - separated into SLANT and EXPOSURE, with the paper reporting that slant mattered less than exposure in this case
span.quote: We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure.

span.label: effect of newspapers - measured on four outcomes that came apart: NO effect on political knowledge, stated opinions, or 2005 turnout; an effect on candidate support; and weaker evidence of an effect on 2006 turnout
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion. Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment. We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure. Some evidence from voting records also suggests that receiving either paper led to increased 2006 voter turnout

span.label: replicates → Gentzkow (2006)
span.quote: Our finding that turnout among the treatment groups was about 3 percentage points higher than the control group is consistent with previous work showing positive turnout effects from newspaper reading (Gentzkow 2006) and suggests newspaper exposure might have an important long term effect on the level of political interest.

span.label: media slant —distinct-from→ media exposure
span.note: differs in: WHICH ONE THE EXPERIMENT COULD MOVE THE OUTCOME WITH. Both papers - the conservative Times and the liberal Post - produced more support for the DEMOCRATIC candidate, so the effect cannot be attributed to slant. The design separates the two by giving opposite slants and finding the same direction · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE FINDING IS A NULL ON THE VARIABLE THE STUDY WAS DESIGNED AROUND. Slant is what the two-newspaper design exists to test, and it is the one thing that did not matter - 'media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure'.
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion. Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment. We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure. Some evidence from voting records also suggests that receiving either paper led to increased 2006 voter turnout

span.label: newspaper provision —causes→ turnout
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — Reported at the weakest grade the paper uses - 'SOME EVIDENCE from voting records ALSO SUGGESTS' - and the record already carries a limitation saying the turnout effect appeared only in 2006 and was of borderline significance.
span.quote: We conducted a field experiment to measure the effect of exposure to newspapers on political behavior and opinion. Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment. We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data. However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure. Some evidence from voting records also suggests that receiving either paper led to increased 2006 voter turnout

span.label: ordinary least squares regression and probit
span.term: ordinary least squares regression and probit
span.quote: All results remain qualitatively similar, and statistical significance remains as-is, using probit or ordered probit specifications instead of OLS. II.

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: Column 5 reports the p-values for chi-squared tests of independence between treatments for each variable.

span.label: multinomial logit regression
span.quote: Using the treatment assignment as the dependent variable in a multinomial logit model produced a p-value for the joint significance of the covariates of p 5 0.95.

span.label: standard error
span.quote: Consequently, the standard errors of the estimated treatment effects were often large.

span.label: null hypothesis significance test / minimum detectable effect
span.term: null hypothesis significance test / minimum detectable effect
span.quote: Our standard errors are such that we fail to reject (two-sided, at the five percent level) the null hypothesis of no effect if we obtain a treatment effect estimate of less than a 3.6 percentage point change in voter turnout (using state voting data), a 7 percentage point increase in likelihood of voting for the Democratic candidate (using survey data), or less than an 8.6 percentage point differential between the Post and Times groups in likelihood of voting for the Democratic candidate.

span.label: standardization by standard deviations from the mean
span.term: standardization by standard deviations from the mean
span.quote: Dependent variables are indexes constructed by summing the standard deviations from the mean for each of the specific questions for each index.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: The lowest p-value for a test of independence across groups was 0.18 (for gender).

span.label: Ten weeks of a free newspaper subscription had no detectable effect on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in the 2005 election.
span.quote: We find no effect of either paper on political knowledge, stated opinions, or turnout in post-election survey and voter data.

span.label: Receiving either newspaper increased support for the Democratic candidate, so exposure to news rather than the paper's slant drove the effect.
span.quote: However, receiving either paper led to more support for the Democratic candidate, suggesting that media slant mattered less in this case than media exposure.

span.label: Receiving the Post raised the probability of voting for the Democrat by 11.2 percentage points among those who voted and by 7.2 percentage points across all respondents.
span.quote: Getting the Post is estimated to increase the probability of selecting the Democrat by 11.2 percentage points ( p , 0.014) among those who reported voting (column 4) and by 7.2 percentage points ( p , 0.043) across all respondents.

span.label: The conservative Washington Times also raised the probability of a Democratic vote, contrary to what a slant-based account predicts.
span.quote: Contrary to initial expectations, the right leaning Times was also associated with an increase in the probability of a Democratic vote in the Virginia governor’s race.

span.label: The estimated effects of the two papers cannot be statistically distinguished from one another.
span.quote: The difference between the Post and Times point estimates is not statistically significant.

span.label: Administrative records show turnout in the 2006 election 2.8 percentage points higher in the treatment groups, an effect of only borderline significance.
span.quote: In November 2006 (column 3), however, the administrative data show a 2.8 percentage point higher voter turnout, with a standard error of 1.6 percentage points (p , 0.11).

span.label: Neither newspaper improved respondents' ability to answer factual questions about recent news, individually or in aggregate.
span.quote: Neither of the newspapers improved the subject’s ability to answer factual questions about the recent news, and no effect is found in aggregate.

span.label: About 17 percent of the Post treatment group chose to buy a subscription after the free ten weeks ended, evidence that the papers were not simply thrown away.
span.quote: The Post informed us that, as of March 2006 (three months after the free subscription ended), approximately 17 percent of the treatment group had decided to subscribe to the Post.

span.label: Randomization succeeded: no baseline characteristic differed significantly across the three groups, the weakest balance being on gender.
span.quote: The lowest p-value for a test of independence across groups was 0.18 (for gender).

span.label: The study is underpowered for small effects: turnout effects below 3.6 points, Democratic-vote effects below 7 points, and Post-versus-Times differences below 8.6 points could not have been detected.
span.quote: Our standard errors are such that we fail to reject (two-sided, at the five percent level) the null hypothesis of no effect if we obtain a treatment effect estimate of less than a 3.6 percentage point change in voter turnout (using state voting data), a 7 percentage point increase in likelihood of voting for the Democratic candidate (using survey data), or less than an 8.6 percentage point differential between the Post and Times groups in likelihood of voting for the Democratic candidate.

span.label: intent to treat effects
span.quote: In our analysis, we focus on intent to treat effects and include all treatment group subjects even if they cancelled.

span.label: Broad Policy index
span.quote: Column 3 is a “Broad Policy” index of four broad political views (Bush’s approval rating, Republican favorable rating, Democrat favorable rating, and respondent’s reported political ideology).

span.label: Specific Issue Index
span.quote: The Specific Issue Index is based on five questions on political issues (three questions about Iraq and the war, a question on the Plame leak, a question about the Alito confirmation).

span.label: free ten-week subscription to the Washington Post or the Washington Times (versus no paper)
span.term: free ten-week subscription to the Washington Post or the Washington Times (versus no paper)
span.quote: Before the 2005 Virginia gubernatorial election, we randomly assigned individuals to a Washington Post free subscription treatment, a Washington Times free subscription treatment, or a control treatment.

span.label: reported vote for the Democratic candidate in the 2005 gubernatorial election
span.term: reported vote for the Democratic candidate in the 2005 gubernatorial election
span.quote: The dependent variables in columns 4 and 5 of Table 4 are dummy variables equal to one if the subject reported voting for the Democratic candidate in the 2005 gubernatorial election.

span.label: voter turnout from state administrative records
span.term: voter turnout from state administrative records
span.quote: For analyzing the effects on voter turnout, we also obtained administrative records of individual voter turnout and successfully merged these data for 2,571 (76.8 percent) of the individuals in the baseline (not all individuals in the sample frame were registered voters).

span.label: factual knowledge index (three news-fact questions)
span.quote: The dependent variable in Table 3, column 1 is an index of whether the respondent correctly answered three factual questions.

span.label: baseline covariates: gender, age, past turnout in 2001/2002/2004, sample frame, magazine subscription
span.term: baseline covariates: gender, age, past turnout in 2001/2002/2004, sample frame, magazine subscription
span.quote: survey. We include the following covariates: gender; reported age; three separate indicators for voting in the 2001, 2002, and 2004 general elections; an indicator for whether the respondent was drawn from a consumer list; self reports of receiving any news or political magazines;

span.label: randomization strata, survey date and surveyor (fixed effects)
span.term: randomization strata, survey date and surveyor (fixed effects)
span.quote: All models include the baseline covariates, and fixed effects for strata, survey date, and surveyor.

span.label: newspaper slant (liberal Post versus conservative Times)
span.term: newspaper slant (liberal Post versus conservative Times)
span.quote: The difference between the Post and Times point estimates is not statistically significant.

span.label: 3,347 — Households that reported taking neither newspaper at baseline and were randomized into the three arms
span.quote: From the 3,347 households reporting that they received neither the Post nor the Times, we randomly assigned households to get subscriptions to either the Post or the Times for approximately ten weeks, or to a control group that was not sent either paper.

span.label: 1,081 / 2,571 — Post-election survey interviews, and the number of subjects matched to administrative voting records
span.quote: The sample size for the post-election survey was 1,081 interviews and the sample size for the data merged with administrative voting records is still only 2,571.

span.label: 11.2 percentage points ( p , 0.014) — Estimated increase in the probability of voting for the Democratic candidate caused by receiving the Washington Post, among those who reported voting
span.quote: Getting the Post is estimated to increase the probability of selecting the Democrat by 11.2 percentage points ( p , 0.014) among those who reported voting (column 4) and by 7.2 percentage points ( p , 0.043) across all respondents.

span.label: 2.8 percentage point — Higher 2006 turnout in the treatment groups in administrative records, standard error 1.6 points
span.quote: In November 2006 (column 3), however, the administrative data show a 2.8 percentage point higher voter turnout, with a standard error of 1.6 percentage points (p , 0.11).

span.label: approximately 17 percent — Share of the Post treatment group that had bought its own subscription three months after the free trial ended
span.quote: The Post informed us that, as of March 2006 (three months after the free subscription ended), approximately 17 percent of the treatment group had decided to subscribe to the Post.

span.label: 6 percent — Share of treatment-group households that cancelled the free subscription, kept in the sample under intent to treat
span.quote: First, 6 percent of households in the treatment groups opted out of the free subscription.

span.label: approximately 92 percentage points — Actual increase in Post exposure produced by the treatment, rather than 100 points, because some control and Times households already received the Post on Sundays
span.quote: this suggests the treatment effect should be interpreted as the effect of boosting the household exposure rate to the Post by approximately 92 percentage points rather than 100 percentage points

span.label: 1,081 of 3,347 — individuals reinterviewed for the post-election follow-up survey
span.quote: During the week after the November election, we reinterviewed 1,081 of the 3,347 individuals in our sample for the follow-up survey.

span.label: 2,571 — sample size for the data merged with administrative voting records, named as a limitation
span.quote: Our study has some important limitations, the most important of which is the relatively small sample size. The sample size for the post-election survey was 1,081 interviews and the sample size for the data merged with administrative voting records is still only 2,571.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1257/app.1.2.35.
